issue: A long-running Bash launcher could be modified in place while blocked in wait, then read changed commands and exit abnormally after GPU work completed.

observed_case.evidence_boundary: The empty historical supervisor.log prevents uniquely reconstructing the exact misread command. Runtime script mutation is the strongest evidence-supported cause, not a mathematically proven unique cause.

remediation: Acceptance launchers use git archive to create a read-only snapshot of the complete tracked source at the launch commit before entering long waits or GPU lock scopes.
The running shell execs the launcher inside that source snapshot, so later repository edits cannot alter its remaining control flow, Python modules, or configs used by later lanes.
The launch commit is propagated explicitly instead of being recomputed after snapshot exec.
AutoFormer supervisor logging records launcher lifecycle, lock acquisition and release, child waits, failing BASH_COMMAND, line, and exit code.
Task-scoped lock holders explicitly unlock immediately after each serial scientific task exits; packed scopes unlock when all concurrently active workloads exit.

runtime_audit_at_recording.interpretation: Persistent lock pathnames are normal; all non-blocking flock probes succeeded.

validation: Regression test rewrites the original launcher to exit 127 during sleep and verifies the commit-snapshotted process still exits 0 and writes both lifecycle markers.
limitations: The lock protocol coordinates only same-user zcp-test processes.
Automatic termination is intentionally not based only on low GPU utilization because CPU preprocessing, checkpointing, or validation may legitimately use little GPU.
A task-scoped holder with an active child retains its lock by design; a serial lane must release and reacquire between tasks.
